newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: In South Korea, PM's office is a revolving door.
newsitem.headline: In South Korea, PM's office is a revolving door.

text.p: By discarding his fifth prime minister in four years on Tuesday, South Korean President Kim Young-sam has given more ammunition to critics who say the job is little more than a lightning rod.
Nobody understands the problem better than Ro Jai-bong, whose six months in the office began in December 1990 under then president Roh Tae-woo.
In South Korea, "name is big, power is small", said Ro, quoting an old proverb.
"The president has all the power, but when the arrow of blame is directed in his direction he turns it around and sends it flying to the prime ministers, and fires them," said Ro.
"At this rate, sooner or later all 40 million South Koreans will have a chance to be prime minister."
Kim's fifth prime minister, legal scholar Lee Soo-sung, made way for Koh Kun on Tuesday. By current standards his career span was remarkable: 15 months, the longest of any of Kim's premiers.

Only Minister of Information Oh In-whan is left from the cabinet Kim named when he took office in February 1993. The rest have been dumped by an administration that has sacrificed scores of ministerial careers as it lurched from one crisis to another.
Last year alone, 17 ministers were shown the door. Two left under a corruption cloud, including former defence minister Lee Yang-ho, now in jail for taking bribes in an arms deal.
Home affairs minister Kim Woo-suk was arrested and detained this year in connection with a loans scandal involving bankrupt Hanbo Steel Co.
A handful of ministers are expected to be dropped in a reshuffle on Wednesday designed to defuse public anger over the Hanbo affair, which cost Kim his reputation as a graft-buster.

"Our country has got into this mess because the president doesn't know how to do his job," said Rhee Sang-woo, an expert on North Korea at Seoul's Sogang University, who said he had turned down numerous cabinet offers.
"I would love to take up a ministerial position. I have many great ideas," he said. "But I would never accept unless I knew I could have real power to implement policies."
So why would anybody accept a cabinet seat?
For the status, acccording to Moon Chung-in, a political science professor at Yonsei University.
"Once a minister always a minister," he said.
Many ministers are plucked from academia but few return to it. All except one of Kim's premiers have gone on to senior roles in the ruling New Korea Party.
"The position of prime minster or cabinet minister is the top of the social ladder. For professors, it boosts their social status," said Moon.
"There is a tradition of seeking scholars that has been handed down from the administration of military dicatators to add legitimacy to the government. That tradition still prevails," Moon added.
Stephen Marvin, head of research at Ssangyong Securities, said cabinet members come and go but few influenced economic policy. Stock markets generally ignored them.
"My guess is they're probably all the same because if they had a radically different view they'd never be appointed."
